rows.fidelity_note:
Let $\mathcal X$ be a real Hilbert space and let $T_0,C$ be bounded linear operators, with $C$ compact. Let $0\le b\le\alpha<\beta$ and $\|T_0\|\le b$, and write $T=T_0+C$. This assertion says that there are $\alpha<r_1<r_2<\beta$, $K>0$, and a bounded projection $P_u$ commuting with $T$, whose range is finite-dimensional, such that $\|T^n(I-P_u)\|\le Kr_1^n$ and $\|P_ux\|\le Kr_2^{-n}\|T^nP_ux\|$ for every natural number $n$ and every $x\in\mathcal X$. The restriction of $T$ maps the range of $P_u$ onto itself. Hence the complement has a controlled forward evolution and the finite-dimensional part has a controlled inverse evolution. The inequalities imply $r_2>0$, so the reciprocal in $r_2^{-n}$ is an ordinary reciprocal. The formulation uses projections and powers rather than a list of complex eigenvalues. It does not impose the existence or size of an unstable eigenvalue. Taking $b=\alpha=e^{-S/4}$ and $\beta=1$ is the application to the period map.

The formal assertion provides a finite-dimensional commuting projection for every compact perturbation of a small bounded operator, without assuming a particular unstable eigenvalue; it is the spectral input rather than the nonlinear stability conclusion.

rows.fidelity_note:
Let $X$ be a complete real Hilbert space. Let $G(t)$, for $t\ge0$, be a strongly continuous semigroup of contractions with $G(0)=I$. Let $K(\tau):X\times X\to X$ be symmetric and bounded bilinear, continuous in $\tau>0$ on each pair of vectors, with $\|K(\tau)\|\le C_K\tau^{-3/4}$ for $0<\tau\le1$ and $G(a)K(\tau)=K(a+\tau)$ for $a\ge0$, $\tau>0$. Let $D_\mu$ be a continuous dilation action for $\mu>0$, with $D_1=I$, $D_\mu D_\nu=D_{\mu\nu}$, $\|D_\mu x\|=\mu^{1/4}\|x\|$, $D_\mu G(\mu t)=G(t)D_\mu$ for $t\ge0$, and $\mu D_\mu K(\mu\tau)(x,y)=K(\tau)(D_\mu x,D_\mu y)$. Assume there is a dense set of $f\in X$ for which $K(\tau)(f,\cdot)$ is compact for every $\tau>0$. The families $G,K,D$ are defined on all real parameters; their analytic bounds and scaling properties hold on the ranges just stated.

Let $\rho$ be a linear isometry of $X$ onto itself commuting with $G,K,D$ for all their real parameters. Let $w:\mathbb R\to X$ be continuous, nonzero at some time, and satisfy $w(s+S)=\rho w(s)$ with $S>0$. Put $\mathcal S(a)=D_{e^{-a}}G(1-e^{-a})$ and $\widetilde K(a)=D_{e^{-a}}K(1-e^{-a})$. For every $a\le s$, assume the integral below exists and $w(s)=\mathcal S(s-a)w(a)+\int_a^s\widetilde K(s-\sigma)(w(\sigma),w(\sigma))\,d\sigma$.

For every dense linear subspace $C'\subset X$ and $t_0>0$, the assertion supplies an integer $k\ge1$ and a real $\theta$ with $\delta=1-e^{-S/k}\le t_0$ and $e^{-S/(4k)}<\theta<1$. Put $\mu=e^{-S/k}$, $Y=C([0,\delta];X)$ with its supremum norm, $u_n^*(\tau)=D_{(1-\tau)^{-1}}w(nS/k-\log(1-\tau))$, $B_\delta(f,g)(\tau)=\int_0^\tau K(\tau-\sigma)(f(\sigma),g(\sigma))\,d\sigma$, $A_n=2B_\delta(u_n^*,\cdot)$, $\Gamma x(\tau)=G(\tau)x$, and $Lv=D_\mu v(\delta)$. It asserts $\|A_n\|\le1/4$ for all nonnegative integers $n$, and supplies a finite dimensional subspace $V\subset X$, a bounded linear $J:X\to X$ with range in $C'$, and a bounded linear map $\mathcal R:\ell^\infty(\mathbb N;Y)\to X\times\ell^\infty(\mathbb N;Y)$. If $(e,z)=\mathcal Rg$, then $e\in V$, $z_0-A_0z_0-\Gamma Je=g_0$ and $z_n-A_nz_n-\theta^{-1}\Gamma Lz_{n-1}=g_n$ for $n\ge1$. This is a statement of the linear correction on successive intervals; the correction of the datum is $Je\in C'$. The smooth compactly supported space $E$ of the paper is represented by $J(V)$ when $C'$ is the corresponding dense data space. The formula uses only positive $k$, $\mu$, $\theta$ and $1-\tau$, so their reciprocals are ordinary ones. The path operators are formally assigned zero if their required continuous realizations do not exist; the analytic construction for $\delta>0$ proves those realizations before using them.

The product norm controlled by $\mathcal R$ is $\max(\|e\|,\sup_n\|z_n\|_Y)$. A bound for the actual datum correction $Je$ also uses $\|J\|$. The assertion concerns sequences of compact-interval paths, whereas Proposition 4.3 is phrased for a global weighted curve.

This formal statement specifies an implication. Defining the implication does not prove it.

The correction component of the linear right inverse lies in a fixed finite-dimensional space; nonlinear stability and the physical norm identification require the subsequent contraction and realization.

The physical Fourier coefficient is $c(n)=a(n)/(1+4\pi^2|n|^2)^{1/2}$. Its squared norm is $\|u\|^2=\sum_n(1+4\pi^2|n|^2)|c(n)|^2$, the inhomogeneous $H^1$ norm; the mean $c(0)$ may be nonzero. The conjugate symmetry is the reality condition and $n\cdot a(n)=0$ is the divergence-free condition. At $n=0$ the latter gives no restriction, which is why nonzero constants are included. The space is a closed real subspace of $\ell^2(\mathbb Z^3;\mathbb C^3)$ and is complete. A nonzero constant has positive formal norm and zero gradient norm, so the mean-zero restriction is essential in (3.16). Equation (3.15) instead uses the homogeneous norm on mean-zero fields of arbitrary period $L$. The distinction matters: the zero Fourier mode contributes to the formal norm, and no variable spatial period is a parameter of an element of the formal space.

The formal unit-torus space uses the inhomogeneous $H^1$ weight $1+4\pi^2|k|^2$ and retains the zero Fourier coefficient; mean zero is not part of that space definition.
rows.name: Breakdown.Periodic.V

rows.fidelity_note: The formal statement is the following regularity property of a realization of $X$ and a bounded linear map $V:X\to L^6$. Let $\varphi\in C^\infty_{c,\rm div}(\mathbb R^3;\mathbb R^3)$, $T_0>0$, and let $u$ be a continuous mild curve in the supplied real Hilbert space $X$ on the closed interval $[0,T_0]$, with $u(0)$ equal to the supplied realization of $\varphi$. Mild means the heat-plus-quadratic Bochner equation, with each time integral convergent. The regularity conclusion gives fields $U,P$ jointly smooth up to the boundary of $[0,T_0]\times\mathbb R^3$, with $U(0)=\varphi$, $\operatorname{div}U=0$ throughout that closed interval and $\partial_tU+(U\cdot\nabla)U=\Delta U-\nabla P$ for $0<t<T_0$. Each $U(t)$ equals $V(u(t))\in L^6(\mathbb R^3;\mathbb R^3)$, for the supplied bounded linear map $V:X\to L^6$ almost everywhere. There are finite constants $A,B$ such that $\int|U(t)|^2\le A$ and $|U(t,x)|,\|D_xU(t,x)\|_{\rm op}\le B$ for all $t\in[0,T_0]$ and $x\in\mathbb R^3$. This whole-space property is proved for the frequency realization of $\dot H^1_{\rm div}(\mathbb R^3)$ used in the paper; it does not contain the periodic assertion in the quoted sentence.

Assume $x\mapsto K(\tau)(f,x)$ is compact for every $\tau>0$ and every $f$ in some dense subset of $\mathcal X$. In the whole-space application $\mathcal X$ is the Fourier realization of $\dot H^1_{\mathrm{div}}(\mathbb R^3)$, $G(t)=e^{t\Delta}$, and $D_\mu f(x)=\sqrt\mu f(\sqrt\mu x)$. rows.fidelity_note:

Assume $K(\tau)(f,\cdot)$ is compact for a dense set of $f$ and every $\tau>0$.

Let $S>0$, let $\rho$ be a surjective linear isometry commuting with $G$, $K$ and $D$, and let $w:\mathbb R\to X$ be continuous, nonzero at some time, with $w(s+S)=\rho w(s)$ and the similarity-time mild equation. Here that equation uses $\mathcal S(a)=D_{e^{-a}}G(1-e^{-a})$ and $\mathcal K(a)=D_{e^{-a}}K(1-e^{-a})$ and reads $w(s)=\mathcal S(s-s_0)w(s_0)+\int_{s_0}^{s}\mathcal K(s-r)(w(r),w(r))\,dr$ for $s_0\le s$.

Fix a positive natural $k$, set $\mu=e^{-S/k}$, $L=1-\mu$, and put $A_n=2\mathcal B_L(u_n,\cdot)$ where $u_n(\sigma)=D_{(1-\sigma)^{-1}}w(nS/k-\log(1-\sigma))$ on $[0,L]$. The formal statement assumes the chosen subdivision and $\|A_n\|\le1/4$; it does not choose that subdivision or state equality with the paper's unsplit trajectory $h_\chi$.

Mild means the heat-plus-quadratic Bochner equation, with each time integral convergent. The regularity conclusion gives fields $U,P$ jointly smooth up to the boundary of $[0,T_0]\times\mathbb R^3$, with $U(0)=\varphi$, $\operatorname{div}U=0$ throughout that closed interval and $\partial_tU+(U\cdot\nabla)U=\Delta U-\nabla P$ for $0<t<T_0$. rows.fidelity_note: Let $X$ be a real Hilbert space. Suppose $G(t)$, $t\ge0$, is a strongly continuous contraction semigroup and $K(\tau)$ is a symmetric bounded bilinear family, continuous on each pair of arguments for $\tau>0$, with $G(s)K(\tau)=K(s+\tau)$ and $\|K(\tau)\|\le C_K\tau^{-3/4}$ for $0<\tau\le1$. For $\mu>0$, suppose the dilations are strongly continuous, $D_1=I$, $D_\mu D_\eta=D_{\mu\eta}$, $\|D_\mu x\|=\mu^{1/4}\|x\|$, $D_\mu G(\mu t)=G(t)D_\mu$ for $t\ge0$, and $\mu D_\mu K(\mu\tau)(x,y)=K(\tau)(D_\mu x,D_\mu y)$ for $\tau>0$. For a dense set of $f\in X$, require $K(\tau)(f,\cdot)$ compact for every $\tau>0$. Let $\rho$ be a surjective linear isometry commuting with $G,K,D$, including their assigned values at all real parameters. Let $S>0$ and let $w:\mathbb R\to X$ be continuous and nonzero somewhere, with $w(s+S)=\rho w(s)$. For $a\le s$, require the Bochner integral to exist and $w(s)=D_{e^{-(s-a)}}G(1-e^{-(s-a)})w(a)+\int_a^sD_{e^{-(s-r)}}K(1-e^{-(s-r)})(w(r),w(r))\,dr$. Fix an integer $k\ge1$, set $\mu=e^{-S/k}$ and $L=1-\mu$, and define $a_n(\sigma)=D_{(1-\sigma)^{-1}}w(nS/k-\log(1-\sigma))$ for $0\le\sigma\le L$. The formal assertion states that $a_n$ is a continuous mild solution on $[0,L]$, $D_\mu a_n(L)=a_{n+1}(0)$ and $a_{n+k}=\rho a_n$. If $\|w(s)\|\le M$ for every real $s$, it also states $\|a_n\|_\infty\le e^{S/(4k)}M$. The paper proves the whole-period identity by induction on $n$ and uses $\lambda=e^{-S}$. The formal assertion instead expresses the corresponding recurrence on the subdivision $S/k$ and gives no whole-period induction formula as a stated conclusion.
rows.name: Breakdown.ProfilePieceStatement
rows.plain: A profile on short time intervals

rows.fidelity_note: For $0<\mu<1$ and continuous curves $a_n:[0,1-\mu]\to X$ in a real Hilbert space with dilations $D_\mu$, the formal reconstruction is $v(t)=D_{\mu^{-n}}a_n(\sigma)$, $n=\lfloor\log(1-t)/\log\mu\rfloor_{\mathbb N}$ and $\sigma=(t-(1-\mu^n))/\mu^n$. On $0\le t<1$ this gives $0\le\sigma<1-\mu$ and $1-t=\mu^n(1-\sigma)$. The natural-number floor is zero on negative inputs. Outside each interval a curve is extended by its endpoint value. With $\mu=\lambda=e^{-S}$, $S>0$, the selected index and local time are the $n,\sigma$ in the paper. The linked item defines the selected curve; the interval-membership and reconstruction identities are proved in the separate joining result. This definition is not itself that existence theorem.
rows.name: Breakdown.MildFramework.gluePieces

rows.fidelity_note: In $X=\dot H^1_{\mathrm{div}}(\mathbb R^3)$, with norm $\|u\|_X=\|\nabla u\|_2$, the formal assertion requires, for $\mu,\eta>0$, $\|D_\mu x\|_X=\mu^{1/4}\|x\|_X$, $D_1=I$, $D_\mu D_\eta=D_{\mu\eta}$ and $D_\mu G(\mu t)=G(t)D_\mu$ for $t\ge0$. Here $D_\mu u(x)=\sqrt\mu\,u(\sqrt\mu x)$ and $G(t)=e^{t\Delta}$. For $\lambda=e^{-S}>0$ and natural $n$, the norm identity gives $\|D_{\lambda^{-n}}x\|=\lambda^{-n/4}\|x\|$. It supplies this scaling factor only; it does not state the interval decomposition or the particular extrema used for $C$ and $c_*$.

rows.name: Breakdown.orbitNorm

rows.fidelity_note: Let $X$ be a real Banach space, $G(t)$ a strongly continuous contraction semigroup for $t\ge0$, and $K(\tau):X\times X\to X$ symmetric bounded bilinear maps. Assume $K(\tau)(f,g)$ depends continuously on $\tau>0$, $G(s)K(\tau)(f,g)=K(s+\tau)(f,g)$ for $s\ge0$, $\tau>0$, and $\|K(\tau)\|\le C_K\tau^{-3/4}$ for $0<\tau\le1$. For two continuous mild solutions on $[a,b]$ (or $[a,b)$) with the same value at $a$, the formal uniqueness theorem proves equality at every time in that interval. Applying it to $u^*$ and zero gives vanishing on $[a,b]$ once $u^*(a)=0$. The further conclusion at earlier times uses the profile recurrence and is not part of uniqueness itself.
rows.name: Breakdown.mildUnique

rows.name: Breakdown.orbitNorm

rows.fidelity_note: For a real normed space $X$ and real $L$, the formal object is $C([0,L];X)$ with its ordinary supremum norm; it is Banach when $X$ is complete. It contains no parameter $\kappa$. The paper's $C_\kappa([0,1);X)$ uses the finite norm $\sup_{0\le t<1}(1-t)^{1/4-\kappa}\|v(t)\|$. The two domains and norms differ; the formal interval construction introduces geometric weights through a sequence of rescaled curves.
rows.name: Breakdown.Piece

rows.fidelity_note: For a bounded linear operator $M$ on a real normed space, a real $\theta$, a prescribed source sequence $c_n$ and an initial value $x_0$, the formal definition is $x_{n+1}=\theta^{-1}(Mx_n+c_n)$ for natural $n$. It has no boundedness or decay conclusion. At $\theta=0$ division is assigned zero; the dichotomy arguments impose $\theta>0$. The paper's formula (4.5) defines a space of continuous curves with a weighted supremum norm on $[0,1)$. The recurrence definition contains no such function space or norm. In applications, geometric normalization of an already given sequence is one part of the interval construction.
rows.name: Breakdown.orbitSeq

rows.fidelity_note: Let $X$ be a real Hilbert space and $M=T_0+C$, where $T_0,C$ are bounded linear operators, $C$ is compact and $\|T_0\|\le b\le\alpha<\beta$ with $b\ge0$. The formal assertion supplies $\alpha<r_1<r_2<\beta$, $K>0$ and a bounded finite-rank projection $P$ such that $PM=MP$, $\|M^n(I-P)\|\le Kr_1^n$ and $\|Px\|\le Kr_2^{-n}\|M^nPx\|$ for all natural $n$ and $x\in X$; $M$ maps $\operatorname{ran}P$ onto itself. The last two properties make the restricted operator $M_{\mathrm u}$ invertible. The linked theorem proves this assertion. For $b=\alpha=e^{-S/4}$ and $\beta=1$, choose $r_1<\Theta<r_2$. The resulting projection and invertibility give the clause in Lemma 4.5, while the geometric estimates provide additional quantitative information. The theorem applies to every such compact perturbation, independently of its origin as a fluid period map.
rows.name: Breakdown.dichotomyHolds

rows.fidelity_note: The formal object $C([0,L];X)$, for a real normed space $X$, carries the unweighted supremum norm on a compact interval. It has no parameter $\kappa$ and does not state the comparison in the paper. For the paper's norm $\|v\|_\kappa=\sup_{0\le t<1}(1-t)^{1/4-\kappa}\|v(t)\|$, the inequalities follow from $0<1-t\le1$ and $0\le\kappa<1/4$. They are a separate arithmetic consequence of that global norm definition.
rows.name: Breakdown.Piece

rows.fidelity_note: Let $X$ be a real Banach space, $G(t)$ a strongly continuous contraction semigroup for $t\ge0$, and $K(\tau):X\times X\to X$ symmetric bounded bilinear maps. Assume $K(\tau)(f,g)$ depends continuously on $\tau>0$, $G(s)K(\tau)(f,g)=K(s+\tau)(f,g)$ for $s\ge0$, $\tau>0$, and $\|K(\tau)\|\le C_K\tau^{-3/4}$ for $0<\tau\le1$. For $T>0$, put $Y=C([0,T];X)$ with its supremum norm and $B_T(f,g)(t)=\int_0^tK(t-r)(f(r),g(r))\,dr$. The formal definition selects the bounded bilinear map with this formula, assigning zero if no such map exists. The compact-interval operator theorem establishes existence, so the assigned zero value is unused under these hypotheses. Only values inside $[0,T]$ are integrated; the value at lag zero affects a set of measure zero. The paper defines $\mathcal B$ on continuous curves on $[0,1)$. For each $0<T<1$, restricting those curves gives exactly this integral formula on $[0,T]$. The formal object has a compact-interval domain, so it does not by itself define one operator on the whole half-open interval.
rows.name: Breakdown.HeatBilinear.pieceBil

rows.fidelity_note: Let $X$ be a real Banach space, $G(t)$ a strongly continuous contraction semigroup for $t\ge0$, and $K(\tau):X\times X\to X$ symmetric bounded bilinear maps. Assume $K(\tau)(f,g)$ depends continuously on $\tau>0$, $G(s)K(\tau)(f,g)=K(s+\tau)(f,g)$ for $s\ge0$, $\tau>0$, and $\|K(\tau)\|\le C_K\tau^{-3/4}$ for $0<\tau\le1$. For $T>0$, the formal assertion specifies $B_T(f,g)(t)=\int_0^tK(t-r)(f(r),g(r))\,dr$ and $\Gamma_Tx(t)=G(t)x$ on $C([0,T];X)$, with $\|\Gamma_T\|\le1$ and $\|B_T\|\le4C_KT^{1/4}$ when $T\le1$. All curve norms here are unweighted supremum norms. The linked theorem proves this assertion. Restriction to each $0<T<1$ verifies the paper's formula at all times $t<1$, but the stated formal operator acts on $C([0,T];X)$, and no operator on curves over the whole half-open interval is stated.
rows.name: Breakdown.pieceOperator

rows.fidelity_note: Let $X,Y$ be real Banach spaces, $k\ge1$, $\theta>0$, and let $\rho:X\to X$ be a surjective linear isometry. Let $A_n:Y\to Y$, $\Gamma:X\to Y$, $E:Y\to X$ and $J,P:X\to X$ be bounded linear maps. Assume $I-A_n$ have uniformly bounded inverses. Set $S_n=E(I-A_n)^{-1}\Gamma$ and $M=\rho^{-1}S_{k-1}\cdots S_0$, and assume $S_{n+k}=\rho S_n\rho^{-1}$, $P^2=P$, $PM=MP$, $PJ=P$. For $0\le r_1<\theta^k<r_2$, require $\|M^n(I-P)\|\le Kr_1^n$, $\|Px\|\le Kr_2^{-n}\|M^nPx\|$ for all $n\ge0,x\in X$, and surjectivity of $M$ on $\operatorname{ran}P$. The formal assertion supplies a bounded linear $\mathcal R:\ell^\infty(Y)\to X\times\ell^\infty(Y)$. For $(e,z)=\mathcal Rg$, it requires $e\in\operatorname{ran}P$, $z_0-A_0z_0-\Gamma Je=g_0$ and $z_n-A_nz_n-\theta^{-1}\Gamma Ez_{n-1}=g_n$ for $n\ge1$. The product norm is $\max(\|e\|,\sup_n\|z_n\|_Y)$. In the fluid application $Y=C([0,L];X)$. The paper's (4.12) specifies one curve $v$ with a prescribed global source $g$ and initial vector $\chi$. The formal assertion instead solves a bounded sequence of coupled interval equations and chooses a projected initial coordinate. It does not state (4.12) for an arbitrary prescribed $\chi$.
rows.name: Breakdown.PeriodicInverseStatement
rows.plain: The inverse of the interval equations

rows.fidelity_note: For a bounded linear operator $M$ on a real normed space, a real $\theta$, a prescribed source sequence $c_n$ and an initial value $x_0$, the formal definition is $x_{n+1}=\theta^{-1}(Mx_n+c_n)$ for natural $n$. It has no boundedness or decay conclusion. At $\theta=0$ division is assigned zero; the dichotomy arguments impose $\theta>0$. For $\theta>0$, the substitutions $\chi_n=\theta^nx_n$ and $f_n=\theta^nc_n$ yield $\chi_{n+1}=M\chi_n+f_n$. The paper's (4.13) instead defines rescaled curves $v_n,g_n$ and derives its forcing $f_n$ from a global source. The recurrence definition presupposes its sequence $c_n$ and defines none of those physical-to-period maps. It is a related discrete formulation only.
rows.name: Breakdown.orbitSeq

rows.fidelity_note: Let $X$ be a real Hilbert space. Suppose $G(t)$, $t\ge0$, is a strongly continuous contraction semigroup and $K(\tau)$ is a symmetric bounded bilinear family, continuous on each pair of arguments for $\tau>0$, with $G(s)K(\tau)=K(s+\tau)$ and $\|K(\tau)\|\le C_K\tau^{-3/4}$ for $0<\tau\le1$. For $\mu>0$, suppose the dilations are strongly continuous, $D_1=I$, $D_\mu D_\eta=D_{\mu\eta}$, $\|D_\mu x\|=\mu^{1/4}\|x\|$, $D_\mu G(\mu t)=G(t)D_\mu$ for $t\ge0$, and $\mu D_\mu K(\mu\tau)(x,y)=K(\tau)(D_\mu x,D_\mu y)$ for $\tau>0$. For a dense set of $f\in X$, require $K(\tau)(f,\cdot)$ compact for every $\tau>0$. Let $\rho$ be a surjective linear isometry commuting with $G,K,D$, including their assigned values at all real parameters. Let $S>0$ and let $w:\mathbb R\to X$ be continuous and nonzero somewhere, with $w(s+S)=\rho w(s)$. For $a\le s$, require the Bochner integral to exist and $w(s)=D_{e^{-(s-a)}}G(1-e^{-(s-a)})w(a)+\int_a^sD_{e^{-(s-r)}}K(1-e^{-(s-r)})(w(r),w(r))\,dr$. For a dense linear subspace $C\subset X$ and $t_0>0$, the formal assertion chooses $k\ge1$, $\mu=e^{-S/k}$, $L=1-\mu\le t_0$ and $\mu^{1/4}<\theta<1$. On $Y=C([0,L];X)$ with its supremum norm, set $a_n(t)=D_{(1-t)^{-1}}w(nS/k-\log(1-t))$, $A_nz(t)=2\int_0^tK(t-r)(a_n(r),z(r))\,dr$, $\Gamma x(t)=G(t)x$, and $Ev=D_\mu v(L)$. It gives $\|A_n\|\le1/4$, a finite-dimensional $V\subset X$, a bounded linear $J:X\to X$ with range in $C$, and a bounded linear $\mathcal R:\ell^\infty(Y)\to X\times\ell^\infty(Y)$. Writing $(e,z)=\mathcal Rg$, the conclusions are $e\in V$, $z_0-A_0z_0-\Gamma Je=g_0$ and $z_n-A_nz_n-\theta^{-1}\Gamma Ez_{n-1}=g_n$ for $n\ge1$. The physical datum correction is $Je\in J(V)$; its bound also uses $\|J\|$. The bounded source sequence $g_n\in Y$ is an input to this inverse. The paper's (4.15) estimates an interval source and a derived endpoint forcing in terms of the norm of one global $C_\kappa$ curve. The formal assertion contains no such global source norm, no formula for that derived forcing, and no claim of the displayed constant's independence from $\chi$.

rows.fidelity_note: Let $X$ be a real Banach space, $G(t)$ a strongly continuous contraction semigroup for $t\ge0$, and $K(\tau):X\times X\to X$ symmetric bounded bilinear maps. rows.fidelity_note: For a bounded linear operator $M$ on a real normed space, a real $\theta$, a prescribed source sequence $c_n$ and an initial value $x_0$, the formal definition is $x_{n+1}=\theta^{-1}(Mx_n+c_n)$ for natural $n$. rows.fidelity_note: For any curve $w:\mathbb R\to X$ in a real Hilbert space with dilation maps $D_\mu$, the formal function is $u_{s_0}(t)=D_{(1-t)^{-1}}w(s_0-\log(1-t))$. On $t<1$ its scale is positive; the definition requires no recurrence, continuity or equation. In the physical realization $D_\mu f(x)=\sqrt\mu f(\sqrt\mu x)$. For $s=-\log(1-t)$, $(1-t)^{-\kappa}=e^{\kappa s}$ on $t<1$. The paper combines this identity with the dilation norm law and a positive profile lower bound to compare $v$ with $u^*$. rows.fidelity_note: Let $X$ be a real Banach space, $G(t)$ a strongly continuous contraction semigroup for $t\ge0$, and $K(\tau):X\times X\to X$ symmetric bounded bilinear maps. Assume $K(\tau)(f,g)$ depends continuously on $\tau>0$, $G(s)K(\tau)(f,g)=K(s+\tau)(f,g)$ for $s\ge0$, $\tau>0$, and $\|K(\tau)\|\le C_K\tau^{-3/4}$ for $0<\tau\le1$. Let $0<T\le1$, $a,v\in C([0,T];X)$ and $x\in X$. Write $B_T(f,g)(t)=\int_0^tK(t-r)(f(r),g(r))\,dr$. The quoted paper assertion is an equivalence on $[0,1)$. The formal assertion gives the implication from the perturbation identity to an exact mild sum on a closed interval of length at most one; it does not state the converse.

rows.fidelity_note: Let $X$ be a real Banach space, $G(t)$ a strongly continuous contraction semigroup for $t\ge0$, and $K(\tau):X\times X\to X$ symmetric bounded bilinear maps. For $\mu>0$, suppose the dilations are strongly continuous, $D_1=I$, $D_\mu D_\eta=D_{\mu\eta}$, $\|D_\mu x\|=\mu^{1/4}\|x\|$, $D_\mu G(\mu t)=G(t)D_\mu$ for $t\ge0$, and $\mu D_\mu K(\mu\tau)(x,y)=K(\tau)(D_\mu x,D_\mu y)$ for $\tau>0$. For a dense set of $f\in X$, require $K(\tau)(f,\cdot)$ compact for every $\tau>0$. Let $\rho$ be a surjective linear isometry commuting with $G,K,D$, including their assigned values at all real parameters. Let $S>0$ and let $w:\mathbb R\to X$ be continuous and nonzero somewhere, with $w(s+S)=\rho w(s)$. For $a\le s$, require the Bochner integral to exist and $w(s)=D_{e^{-(s-a)}}G(1-e^{-(s-a)})w(a)+\int_a^sD_{e^{-(s-r)}}K(1-e^{-(s-r)})(w(r),w(r))\,dr$. Fix an integer $k\ge1$, put $\mu=e^{-S/k}$, $L=1-\mu$ and $a_n(t)=D_{(1-t)^{-1}}w(nS/k-\log(1-t))$ on $[0,L]$. On $Y=C([0,L];X)$ define $A_nz(t)=2\int_0^tK(t-r)(a_n(r),z(r))\,dr$, $\Gamma x(t)=G(t)x$ and $Ev=D_\mu v(L)$. The formal assertion assumes $\|A_n\|\le1/4$ for every $n$, and states that $I-A_n$ is invertible with inverse norm at most $4/3$. With $S_n=E(I-A_n)^{-1}\Gamma$, $\mathcal M=\rho^{-1}S_{k-1}\cdots S_0$ and $\mathcal M_0=\rho^{-1}(D_\mu G(L))^k$, it states $S_{n+k}=\rho S_n\rho^{-1}$, compactness of $\mathcal M-\mathcal M_0$, and $\|\mathcal M_0\|\le e^{-S/4}$. It does not state the separate identification of its product with the paper's whole-period trajectory. Thus the displayed conclusions correspond after additional identifications, while the full statements have different hypotheses and formulations.

rows.fidelity_note:
Assume the radial-potential assertion that every smooth solenoidal $g$ has a smooth potential $A_{x_0,g}$ with $\operatorname{curl}A_{x_0,g}=g$. For every smooth scalar function $\chi:\mathbb R^3\to\mathbb R$, every centre $x_0$ and every smooth solenoidal vector field $g$, the formal statement then proves that $\bar g=\chi g+\nabla\chi\times A_{x_0,g}$ is smooth and $\nabla\cdot\bar g=0$ at every point. Here $A_{x_0,g}(x)=\int_0^1\sigma\,g(x_0+\sigma(x-x_0))\times(x-x_0)\,d\sigma$. In §5 take $x_0=0$, $g=u^*(t)$ and $\chi(x)=\eta(x/r)$ with $r>0$. This theorem assumes no support or size conditions on $\chi$ and therefore gives no support radius, no equality on an inner ball, and no norm bound. Its radial-potential premise is proved in the preceding curl theorem.

For a smooth solenoidal field and a smooth scalar cutoff, the formal statement proves that the vector-potential cutoff is smooth and solenoidal; take the centre to be zero and the scalar cutoff to be $\eta(x/r)$.

rows.fidelity_note:
Let $W:\mathbb R\times\mathbb R^3\to\mathbb R^3$ and $q:\mathbb R\times\mathbb R^3\to\mathbb R$ be smooth and satisfy $\partial_sW+\frac12W+\frac12(y\cdot\nabla)W-\Delta W+(W\cdot\nabla)W+\nabla q=0$ and $\nabla\cdot W=0$ for every $(s,y)$. Assume, uniformly in $s,y$, $\|D_y^jW(s,y)\|_{\rm op}\le C(1+|y|)^{-j-1}$ for the three integer orders $j=0,1,2$, and $|\nabla_yq(s,y)|\le C(1+|y|)^{-3}$. These assumptions imply $C\ge0$; recurrence and nonvanishing are not required here. The norm on a first derivative is its operator norm; the paper's pointwise matrix norm is the square root of the sum of the squared column lengths, which is at most $\sqrt3$ times this norm.

Put $a=(1/2,1/2,1/2)$ and let $\chi$ be the fixed smooth cutoff with $0\le\chi\le1$, equal to one for $|x-a|\le1/16$ and zero for $|x-a|\ge1/8$. For $T>0$, $t<T$, set $\ell=T-t$, $s=-\log(\ell/T)$ and $g(x)=\ell^{-1/2}W(s,(x-a)/\sqrt\ell)$. Define $A_g(x)=\int_0^1\sigma\,g(a+\sigma(x-a))\times(x-a)\,d\sigma$, $\bar u(x)=\chi(x)g(x)+\nabla\chi(x)\times A_g(x)$, and $f(y)=\sqrt\ell\,\bar u(a+\sqrt\ell\,y)$. Thus $f$ is the cutoff expressed in similarity coordinates; its inner and outer radii are $1/(16\sqrt\ell)$ and $1/(8\sqrt\ell)$. Put $x_a=a+(3/32)e_1$ and $\bar p(x)=\chi(x)\ell^{-1}[q(s,(x-a)/\sqrt\ell)-q(s,(x_a-a)/\sqrt\ell)]$.

For every $T>0$, the formal statement proves that $(t,x)\mapsto\bar u(t,x)$ is smooth on $(-\infty,T)\times\mathbb R^3$, is divergence-free, vanishes for $|x-a|\ge1/8$, and equals $g$ for $|x-a|\le1/16$. It also proves smoothness and the same outer support for $\bar p(t,x)=\chi(x)[\ell^{-1}q(s,(x-a)/\sqrt\ell)-\ell^{-1}q(s,(x_a-a)/\sqrt\ell)]$, where $x_a=a+(3/32)e_1$ is fixed. Thus each spatial cutoff is in $C^\infty_{c,\mathrm{div}}$. The centre, radii, time interval and pressure normalization are fixed as stated; an arbitrary radius $r$ is absent from the assertion. All logarithms, square roots and quotients used for $t<T$, $T>0$ have their ordinary positive arguments. The result gives no quantitative norm estimate.

The formal statement proves smoothness for $t<T$ and support and agreement for the translated cutoff with radii $1/8,1/16$; the paper fixes terminal time one, centre zero and every radius $r>0$.
rows.name: Breakdown.Periodic.approxFieldProperties_holds
rows.plain: Support and agreement of the cutoff

rows.fidelity_note:
Let $W:\mathbb R\times\mathbb R^3\to\mathbb R^3$ and $q:\mathbb R\times\mathbb R^3\to\mathbb R$ be smooth, with $\operatorname{div}W=0$ and
$\displaystyle \partial_sW+\tfrac12W+\tfrac12(y\cdot\nabla)W-\Delta W+(W\cdot\nabla)W+\nabla q=0.$
Assume one constant $C$ bounds $\|D_y^jW(s,y)\|_{\mathrm{op}}\le C(1+|y|)^{-j-1}$ for the integer orders $j=0,1,2$, and $|\nabla q(s,y)|\le C(1+|y|)^{-3}$, for every real $s$ and every $y$. Recurrence and nonvanishing are unnecessary here. The first-derivative operator norm differs from the paper's Frobenius norm by a factor at most $\sqrt3$.

Fix $a=(1/2,1/2,1/2)$ and the smooth scalar cutoff $\chi$, equal to one on $\bar B_{1/16}(a)$, zero for $|x-a|\ge1/8$, and taking values in $[0,1]$. For $T>0$ and $t<T$, put $h=T-t$ and $s=\log(T/h)$. Define $u_T^*(t,x)=h^{-1/2}W(s,(x-a)/\sqrt h)$ and
$\displaystyle A_g(x)=\int_0^1\sigma g(a+\sigma(x-a))\times(x-a)\,d\sigma,\qquad \bar u_T(t)=\chi u_T^*(t)+\nabla\chi\times A_{u_T^*(t)}.$
The rescaled cutoff is $f_{T,t}(y)=\sqrt h\,\bar u_T(t,a+\sqrt h\,y)$; its outer and inner radii are $r=1/(8\sqrt h)$ and $r/2$.

Conditional on the stated smoothness, support and inner-agreement properties of this cutoff for every profile, the formal theorem says: for each $\varepsilon>0$ there is $h_0>0$ such that for every $T>0$ and every $t<T$ with $T-t<h_0$,
$\displaystyle \int_{\mathbb R^3}|\nabla(W(s,y)-f_{T,t}(y))|^2\,dy\le\varepsilon.$
The threshold may depend on the profile and $\varepsilon$, and is uniform in $T,t$. The conclusion is qualitative and contains no explicit power of $r$.

The formal statement makes the squared gradient error in similarity coordinates at most any prescribed $\varepsilon>0$ once $T-t$ is small enough; it has no $r^{-1/2}$ rate or bound for every $r>0$.

For each nonnegative integer $n$, let $G_n$ and $K_n$ be a strongly continuous contraction heat semigroup and a symmetric bilinear kernel with positive-lag continuity, $G_n(a)K_n(\tau)=K_n(a+\tau)$ for $a\ge0$, $\tau>0$, and $\|K_n(\tau)\|\le C_K\tau^{-3/4}$ for $0<\tau\le1$. Write $\mathcal B_n(f,g)(s)=\int_0^sK_n(s-\sigma)(f(\sigma),g(\sigma))\,d\sigma$.

Take continuous $a_n,r_n:[0,\ell]\to X$, uniformly bounded $a_n$, with $a_{n+1}(0)=ca_n(\ell)$,
$\displaystyle a_n=G_n(\cdot)a_n(0)+\mathcal B_n(a_n,a_n)+r_n,\qquad\|r_n\|_\infty\le\theta^n\rho.$
Suppose a bounded linear map $R:\ell^\infty(C([0,\ell];X))\to E\times\ell^\infty(C([0,\ell];X))$ has the following right-inverse property: for each $g$, if $(e,z)=Rg$, then
$\displaystyle z_0-2\mathcal B_0(a_0,z_0)-G_0(\cdot)Je=g_0,$
$\displaystyle z_n-2\mathcal B_n(a_n,z_n)-(c/\theta)G_n(\cdot)z_{n-1}(\ell)=g_n\quad(n\ge1).$
The sequence norm is the supremum over $n$ and interval time, and the product norm is the maximum norm. For $\xi\in X$, assume $64\|R\|^2C_K\ell^{1/4}(\rho+\|\xi\|)\le1$. The formal assertion gives $e\in E$ and continuous curves $z_n$, each bounded in norm by $2\|R\|(\rho+\|\xi\|)$, with the same bound for $\|e\|$, such that $a_n+\theta^nz_n$ is exactly mild on $[0,\ell]$, the corrected endpoints match with factor $c$, and $z_0(0)=\xi+Je$. No finite-dimensional hypothesis is imposed on $E$.

The formal correction is carried out on normalized intervals of the unit torus, with an explicit quadratic smallness condition. It does not first construct a global solution on a torus of large period.

Write $a=(1/2,1/2,1/2)$ and let $w(x)$ reduce each coordinate of $x$ modulo integers to the cell centered at $a$. For $\mu>0$, the transplanted field is $g_\mu(x)=\mu^{-1/2}g((w(x)-a)/\sqrt\mu)$.

This is a function on all of $\mathbb R^3$, with period one in each coordinate. When $g$ is supported in $\bar B_b$ and $\sqrt\mu b\le1/8$, its periodic copies have disjoint supports. It is then the translated and rescaled version of the paper’s periodization.

The definition itself imposes neither support nor smoothness. Reciprocal and square root are defined for all real inputs; for $\mu\le0$ the square root and its reciprocal are zero, so this field is zero. Statements using the physical dilation assume $\mu>0$.

The paper sums translates separated by $L$. The formal definition reduces coordinates modulo one and applies $\mu^{-1/2}f((x-a)/\sqrt\mu)$, with center $a=(1/2,1/2,1/2)$; disjoint support makes it the corresponding scaled periodization.

rows.fidelity_note:

This theorem assumes five representation identities. First, for every invertible real linear change of frequency variables $A$ and every strongly measurable uniformly bounded matrix multiplier $M(\xi)$, the selected $L^2$ operator agrees almost everywhere with $f\mapsto[\xi\mapsto M(\xi)f(A\xi)]$. Second, the $L^2$ Fourier transform of an $L^1\cap L^2$ complex vector field agrees almost everywhere with its Fourier integral. Third, the Fourier transform of a real $L^2$ vector field satisfies $\widehat f(-\xi)=\overline{\widehat f(\xi)}$. Fourth, if two solenoidal Fourier representatives satisfy $h(\xi)=2\pi|\xi|g(\xi)$ almost everywhere, the velocity reconstructed from $h$ is the real inverse Fourier transform of $g$. Fifth, the inverse $L^2$ Fourier transform of an $L^1\cap L^2$ field agrees almost everywhere with its inverse Fourier integral. The Fourier convention is $\widehat f(\xi)=\int e^{-2\pi i\xi\cdot x}f(x)\,dx$. These are hypotheses of this particular proof theorem; the main construction supplies their proofs.

The whole-space norm is $\|v\|_X=\|\nabla v\|_{L^2(\mathbb R^3)}$ on solenoidal velocities in $L^6(\mathbb R^3)$.

Local data are a tuple $(A_1,A_2,A_3,v)$ with $A_j\in L^2(\mathbb R^3;\mathbb R^3)$ and $v\in L^6(\mathbb R^3;\mathbb R^3)$, measured by $\max\{\max_j\|A_j\|_2,\|v\|_6\}$. No compatibility condition $A_j=\partial_jv$ or divergence condition is part of this data space.

Let $a=(1/2,1/2,1/2)$ and let $w(x)$ reduce coordinates modulo integers to the unit cell centered at $a$. Whole-space restriction to $\bar B_b$ consists of $1_{\bar B_b}\partial_jv$ and $1_{\bar B_b}v$. At an admissible periodic scale $0<\mu\le1$, $b>0$, $\sqrt\mu\,b\le1/8$, periodic restriction consists of $1_{\bar B_b}\mu^{3/4}\partial_jz(a+\sqrt\mu\,y)$ and $1_{\bar B_b}\mu^{1/4}z(a+\sqrt\mu\,y)$, interpreted almost everywhere. It is defined to be zero if these scale conditions fail.

Given $b,b^{\prime},\varepsilon,\delta>0$, the formal statement asserts the existence of $\mu_0>0$ such that, for $0<\mu<\mu_0$, every $\tau\in[\varepsilon,\varepsilon^{-1}]$ and every $A\in L^2(\mathbb R^3;\mathbb R^3)$ supported almost everywhere in $\bar B_{b^{\prime}}$, the difference between the restricted whole-space field $e^{\tau\Delta}\mathbb PA$ and the restricted rescaled unit-torus field is at most $\delta\|A\|_{3/2}$. The latter field is $\mu^{-1/4}e^{\mu\tau\Delta}\mathbb P[A((w(x)-a)/\sqrt\mu)]$ before the periodic restriction. Compact support makes $\|A\|_{3/2}$ finite. If $\varepsilon>1$, the time interval is empty. The statement has no explicit rate in $\mu$ and no assertion for all positive times. Lemma 6.1 instead assumes a tensor $F\in W^{1,1}$ and bounds the heat flow of $\operatorname{div}F$ by $CL^{-7/2}\|F\|_1$.

The formal comparison takes a compactly supported $L^2$ vector field as forcing. The paper takes the divergence of a $W^{1,1}$ tensor, which need not lie in $L^2$, and requires a quantitative comparison on a full period cell.

ties.plain: Support and agreement of the cutoff

rows.fidelity_note:
Let $W:\mathbb R\times\mathbb R^3\to\mathbb R^3$ and $q:\mathbb R\times\mathbb R^3\to\mathbb R$ be smooth and satisfy $\partial_sW+\frac12W+\frac12(y\cdot\nabla)W-\Delta W+(W\cdot\nabla)W+\nabla q=0$ and $\nabla\cdot W=0$ for every $(s,y)$. Assume, uniformly in $s,y$, $\|D_y^jW(s,y)\|_{\rm op}\le C(1+|y|)^{-j-1}$ for the three integer orders $j=0,1,2$, and $|\nabla_yq(s,y)|\le C(1+|y|)^{-3}$. These assumptions imply $C\ge0$; recurrence and nonvanishing are not required here. The norm on a first derivative is its operator norm; the paper's pointwise matrix norm is the square root of the sum of the squared column lengths, which is at most $\sqrt3$ times this norm.

Put $a=(1/2,1/2,1/2)$ and let $\chi$ be the fixed smooth cutoff with $0\le\chi\le1$, equal to one for $|x-a|\le1/16$ and zero for $|x-a|\ge1/8$. For $T>0$, $t<T$, set $\ell=T-t$, $s=-\log(\ell/T)$ and $g(x)=\ell^{-1/2}W(s,(x-a)/\sqrt\ell)$. Define $A_g(x)=\int_0^1\sigma\,g(a+\sigma(x-a))\times(x-a)\,d\sigma$, $\bar u(x)=\chi(x)g(x)+\nabla\chi(x)\times A_g(x)$, and $f(y)=\sqrt\ell\,\bar u(a+\sqrt\ell\,y)$. Thus $f$ is the cutoff expressed in similarity coordinates; its inner and outer radii are $1/(16\sqrt\ell)$ and $1/(8\sqrt\ell)$. Put $x_a=a+(3/32)e_1$ and $\bar p(x)=\chi(x)\ell^{-1}[q(s,(x-a)/\sqrt\ell)-q(s,(x_a-a)/\sqrt\ell)]$.

For every $T>0$, the formal statement proves that $(t,x)\mapsto\bar u(t,x)$ is smooth on $(-\infty,T)\times\mathbb R^3$, is divergence-free, vanishes for $|x-a|\ge1/8$, and equals $g$ for $|x-a|\le1/16$. It also proves smoothness and the same outer support for $\bar p(t,x)=\chi(x)[\ell^{-1}q(s,(x-a)/\sqrt\ell)-\ell^{-1}q(s,(x_a-a)/\sqrt\ell)]$, where $x_a=a+(3/32)e_1$ is fixed. Thus each spatial cutoff is in $C^\infty_{c,\mathrm{div}}$. The centre, radii, time interval and pressure normalization are fixed as stated; an arbitrary radius $r$ is absent from the assertion. All logarithms, square roots and quotients used for $t<T$, $T>0$ have their ordinary positive arguments. The result gives no quantitative norm estimate.

The formal theorem applies the solenoidal cutoff after scaling to the unit cell: it agrees with the centered self-similar field on radius $1/16$ and vanishes outside radius $1/8$, for all $t<T$. The paper states the corresponding radii $L/16,L/8$ on the large torus.

rows.plain: Support and agreement of the cutoff

rows.fidelity_note:
Let $W:\mathbb R\times\mathbb R^3\to\mathbb R^3$ and $q:\mathbb R\times\mathbb R^3\to\mathbb R$ be smooth, with $\operatorname{div}W=0$ and
$\displaystyle \partial_sW+\tfrac12W+\tfrac12(y\cdot\nabla)W-\Delta W+(W\cdot\nabla)W+\nabla q=0.$
Assume one constant $C$ bounds $\|D_y^jW(s,y)\|_{\mathrm{op}}\le C(1+|y|)^{-j-1}$ for the integer orders $j=0,1,2$, and $|\nabla q(s,y)|\le C(1+|y|)^{-3}$, for every real $s$ and every $y$. Recurrence and nonvanishing are unnecessary here. The first-derivative operator norm differs from the paper's Frobenius norm by a factor at most $\sqrt3$.

Fix $a=(1/2,1/2,1/2)$ and the smooth scalar cutoff $\chi$, equal to one on $\bar B_{1/16}(a)$, zero for $|x-a|\ge1/8$, and taking values in $[0,1]$. For $T>0$ and $t<T$, put $h=T-t$ and $s=\log(T/h)$. Define $u_T^*(t,x)=h^{-1/2}W(s,(x-a)/\sqrt h)$ and
$\displaystyle A_g(x)=\int_0^1\sigma g(a+\sigma(x-a))\times(x-a)\,d\sigma,\qquad \bar u_T(t)=\chi u_T^*(t)+\nabla\chi\times A_{u_T^*(t)}.$
The rescaled cutoff is $f_{T,t}(y)=\sqrt h\,\bar u_T(t,a+\sqrt h\,y)$; its outer and inner radii are $r=1/(8\sqrt h)$ and $r/2$.

Conditional on the stated smoothness, support and inner-agreement properties of this cutoff for every profile, the formal theorem says: for each $\varepsilon>0$ there is $h_0>0$ such that for every $T>0$ and every $t<T$ with $T-t<h_0$,
$\displaystyle \int_{\mathbb R^3}|\nabla(W(s,y)-f_{T,t}(y))|^2\,dy\le\varepsilon.$
The threshold may depend on the profile and $\varepsilon$, and is uniform in $T,t$. The conclusion is qualitative and contains no explicit power of $r$.

The formal theorem controls the squared gradient error in similarity coordinates by arbitrary $\varepsilon$ for sufficiently small $T-t$. It does not export the explicit radius estimate $CL^{-1/2}$. This linked statement addresses only the gradient estimate; the $L^2$ bound is the other assertion in the numbered display.

rows.fidelity_note:
Assume that $W:\mathbb R\times\mathbb R^3\to\mathbb R^3$ and $q:\mathbb R\times\mathbb R^3\to\mathbb R$ are smooth, that $\operatorname{div}W=0$, and that $\partial_sW+\tfrac12W+\tfrac12(y\cdot\nabla)W-\Delta W+(W\cdot\nabla)W+\nabla q=0$ for every $(s,y)$. A single constant $C$ bounds $\|D^jW(s,y)\|\le C(1+|y|)^{-j-1}$ for the integer orders $j=0,1,2$, and $|\nabla q(s,y)|\le C(1+|y|)^{-3}$, uniformly in $s$. The norms of $D^jW$ are multilinear operator norms; for $j=1$ the paper’s Frobenius norm is between the operator norm and $\sqrt3$ times that norm.

The periodic space is the real solenoidal Fourier realization of $H^1(\mathbb R^3/\mathbb Z^3)$, with squared norm $\sum_{k\in\mathbb Z^3}(1+4\pi^2|k|^2)|\widehat v(k)|^2$. Its zero Fourier coefficient is allowed to be nonzero.

For $T>0$ and $t<T$, put $s=\log(T/(T-t))$ and $u_T^*(t,x)=(T-t)^{-1/2}W(s,(x-a)/\sqrt{T-t})$, where $a=(1/2,1/2,1/2)$. Choose a fixed smooth cutoff $\chi$, equal to one on $\bar B_{1/16}(a)$ and zero when $|x-a|\ge1/8$. Put $A_g(x)=\int_0^1\tau g(a+\tau(x-a))\times(x-a)\,d\tau$. The cutoff is $\bar u_T=\chi u_T^*+\nabla\chi\times A_{u_T^*}$, which equals $\operatorname{curl}(\chi A_{u_T^*})$ when $u_T^*$ is solenoidal.

Write $\mu_n=T\lambda^n$, $t_n=T-\mu_n$, $\ell=1-\lambda$, and $a_n(s)=\mu_n^{1/4}u^{\mathrm a}(t_n+\mu_ns)$ for $0\le s\le\ell$, where $u^{\mathrm a}$ is the unit-periodic extension of the solenoidal cutoff of the centered self-similar field. The index $n$ is a nonnegative integer and the interval norm is the supremum norm.

For $0<T\le1$ and $0<\lambda<1$, the formal statement proves the defining formula for every $a_n$ throughout $[0,\ell]$ and the endpoint identity $a_{n+1}(0)=\lambda^{1/4}a_n(\ell)$. The time intervals are $[T-T\lambda^n,T-T\lambda^{n+1}]$, and the factor in the endpoint identity comes from their amplitude normalizations. Values used outside a closed interval are extended by the endpoint values. This supplies the matching needed to assemble continuous physical curves.

The formal theorem establishes continuous normalized interval representatives and their endpoint matching for the scaled unit-periodic approximation. The paper’s sentence concerns the unperiodized cutoff as one whole-space curve.

Put $a=(1/2,1/2,1/2)$, and let $w(x)$ be coordinatewise reduction modulo $\mathbb Z^3$ to the unit cell centred at $a$. For $\mu>0$, define $g_\mu(x)=\mu^{-1/2}g((w(x)-a)/\sqrt\mu)$. It specifies neither a correction space nor a two-sided rate nor a norm of the difference from the self-similar profile.

The formal final assertion is smooth periodic data with a mild trajectory of unbounded $H^1$ norm before a positive time. Proposition 2.2 additionally gives a two-sided blow-up rate and an $H^1(B_{1/16})$ estimate relative to the self-similar profile.

rows.fidelity_note:
The second conclusion of Lemma B.6 is treated by a separate formal result. Fix $\alpha\in\mathcal K$ and the multiplier data described below. The exterior $Z$ is either $\{r>0,z>0:ho>R(r,z)\}$, with $ho=\sqrt{r^2+z^2}$ and a measurable degree-zero homogeneous radius $0<R_0\le R\le R_1$, or $\{r>0,z>0:r>a	ext{ or }z>a\}$ with $a>0$. A harmonic set has $|\varkappa\iota_1|\ge k_0$; in the square case every allowed harmonic has zero azimuthal frequency and obeys $\hat v_\iota(r,-z)=R_*\hat v_{\iota^ lat}(r,z)$ almost everywhere. Uniform lower square coefficients $f_2,f'_2,f'_1,f_1,f_0$ and an upper mixed coefficient $f_{01}$ are supplied after subtraction of stretching and other charges, through the regional class, membership and interaction bounds. Let $f_1^*=f_1+2\min(f'_1+f'_2(k_0-1)_+^2/r^2,0)+f_2(k_0-2)_+^2/r^2$. Require $f_2\ge0$, $f_1^*\ge f_1^\infty$, $ho^2(-f_0)_+\le f_0^\infty$, $ho f_{01}\le f_{01}^\infty$, and $f_0^\infty,f_{01}^\infty\ge0$. For some $\Lambda_0>0$, require $f_0^\infty/\Lambda_0+f_{01}^\infty/\sqrt{\Lambda_0}\le f_1^\infty$ and $\Lambda_0\le rac14+(k_0-1)_+^2$ on a ray exterior or $\Lambda_0\le2$ on a square exterior.
